A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLEF and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. Corresponding content can be matched reliably, including v1 Table 4 becoming v2 Table 4a.

before.justification: V1 reports original RLEF evaluations on CodeContests, HumanEval+, and MBPP+, together with training ablations, feedback analyses, and code-repair examples.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds repair-model, feedback-removal, and value-function comparisons in Appendices B.3–B.5.

M1.justification: Section 2.2 revises the specified PPO advantage from current-step reward minus value to cumulative remaining rewards minus value. The iterative generation procedure, reward components, and model architecture remain unchanged. This establishes a change in the written training formulation; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed. The newly detailed clipped value loss was already mentioned in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use CodeContests for training and competitive-programming evaluation, with HumanEval+ and MBPP+ for transfer evaluation. The added repair and training controls remain within the existing Python code-generation and repair coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix B.3 and Table 4b add a separately trained repair model paired with single-turn RL. Table 4b also compares feedback-free training and a token-level value-function variant against RLEF. The external comparator sets in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 3.1 changes the reported training filter from 115 problems missing public tests to 669 missing public or private tests. Appendix A.3 changes one SFT learning rate from 5e-7 to 5e-6, while B.2 changes execution from all available tests to 20 tests. New appendix protocols include separate-repair evaluation and three-response training without feedback or early stopping. Reruns of retained experiments are not established.

E4.justification: Appendices B.3–B.5 substantially expand checks of the training design: separate generation and repair models, removal of public-test feedback and early stopping, and token-level versus response-level value estimation. These complement v1's existing inference-feedback, turn-limit, and training-method analyses. B.4 changes feedback and stopping jointly, limiting attribution to feedback alone.

E5.justification: The stated 200-rollout estimates for Table 1 and 20-rollout evaluations for Table 2 and Figure 3 are retained. V2 adds no seed information, repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the former Table 4 retain their scores. New Table 4b reports validation/test 1@3 scores of 14.8/12.6 for separate repair, 12.2/10.9 without feedback, and 13.1/13.7 with token-level values. B.2 revises the 70B public/expanded-feedback validation comparison from 34.0/36.8 to 37.5/40.4 and the expanded-feedback test score from 40.9 to 41.2. Its changed test-case protocol prevents treating these as established same-setting gains.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the advantage definition to include cumulative remaining rewards. Appendix A.1 adds explicit reward-to-go and clipped value-loss equations where v1 only mentioned a clipped value loss. These are localized mathematical corrections and specifications; the POMDP assumptions remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: learning to exploit execution feedback, strong CodeContests results with smaller sampling budgets, and generalization to other benchmarks and longer interactions. The added experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: The conclusion newly acknowledges that required unit tests may be unavailable and proposes automatic test generation as future work. V1's limitation concerning larger tasks requiring decomposition, and its interpretations of diversity and targeted repair, remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly specifies advantage normalization and value clipping with threshold 0.2. B.3 documents repair-data construction from 1.48 million failed generations, solution verification and indentation processing, training hyperparameters, and checkpoint selection. Existing hardware, runtime, execution-code access information, and prompt templates are retained.

R1.justification: Section 4 revises its account of Le et al.'s critic and repair models and emphasizes RLEF's use of one model for generation and repair. It adds discussion or citations for StepCoder, RLTF, B-Coder, and natural-language-feedback training. Unit-test-generation references support the new limitation. The overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized wording and punctuation corrections, revises part of related work, and adds an appendix-results summary in Section 3.4.2. Quentin Carbonneaux moves from acknowledgements to the author list. Appendix B gains three subsections, while the overall section order and most existing prose remain.

P2.justification: Table 4 becomes a two-panel display, preserving previous results as 4a and adding comparisons as 4b. Table 1 expands the equivalent notation 1k to 1000, and some captions and page layouts change locally. Figures 1–4 retain their graphics.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens support for the existing training design through B.3–B.5, corrects the stated advantage formulation, and improves implementation detail and discussion of test availability. These are useful gains while headline results remain unchanged. Their significance is limited by the joint feedback/early-stopping ablation and numerical inconsistencies, including B.4's initial-model test score of 10.2 versus 10.5 in Table 1.
